Abstract 23

Plasma proteomic signatures accurately predict disease risk, but our understanding of the mechanisms 24

contributing to the predictive value of the proteome remains limited. Here, we characterized proteomic 25

biomarkers of 19 age-related diseases, based on observational associations between 2,923 protein levels and 26

incidence of these outcomes in the UK Biobank (N = 45,438). To identify the subset of these biomarkers that 27

may represent causal drivers of disease, we first employed Mendelian Randomization (MR) and found that only 28

8% of the protein-disease associations with genetic instruments showed suggestive evidence of causal 29

relationships, and were more likely to pertain to only a single disease. We then tested the hypothesis that many 30

proteomic biomarkers, particularly the non-causal proteins, are impacted by environmental factors that might 31

independently affect disease risk and protein levels. We discovered that the vast majority (>90%) of proteins 32

associated with diseases like lung cancer and COPD are also associated with smoking, and more than half of 33

all disease-associated proteins tested in MR were associated with smoking. These proteins showed no evidence 34

of causal effects on disease, suggesting their predictive value is as an environmental sensor. Given the sensitivity 35

of the plasma proteome to smoking, we developed a proteomic score for smoking (SmokingPS) and 36

demonstrated that the plasma proteome can serve as a quantitative index of smoking behavior and history. 37

Extending this approach to alcohol intake phenotypes, our results generally suggest that many plasma proteins 38

identified in observational associations are more likely to be readouts of environmental risk factors than disease- 39

specific signals. We conclude that the plasma proteome may provide critical objective biomarkers for quantifying 40

the impacts of environmental risk factors on human health and disease. Our results have significant implications 41

for implementing predictive plasma protein biomarkers in disease prevention, and can help guide interpretation 42

of putative protein-disease associations as actionable therapeutic targets or quantitative indications of upstream 43

exposures that represent potential intervention points. 44

Introduction 45

Technological advances in high-throughput, broad-capture proteomic assays have highlighted the potential of 46

leveraging plasma proteins for disease prediction, biomarker discovery, and therapeutic development. In the 47

past few years, population-scale biobanks have used these assays to profile portions of the plasma proteome in 48

thousands of individuals1–5. The UK Biobank Pharma Proteomics Project (UKB-PPP) generated one of the 49

largest proteomic resources to date, with measurements of nearly 3,000 blood plasma analytes in more than 50

54,000 UKB participants using the Olink Explore 3072 proximity extension assay6. Coupled with existing deep 51

phenotyping data, UKB-PPP creates a unique opportunity to interrogate the links between the plasma proteome 52

and a broad spectrum of diseases and disease-related traits. Indeed, studies have already leveraged this 53

resource to identify thousands of associations between plasma protein levels and disease outcomes7–9. 54

Proteomic predictors of incident disease, developed from these associations, outperform traditional clinical 55

models and polygenic risk scores for a wide range of diseases7,8,10 (e.g. AUC > 0.8 for 92 diseases9). 56

57

The ability of the plasma proteome to predict incident disease is promising for a range of clinical applications – 58

for example building on ELISA (enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay) and other multiplex immunoassays for 59

diagnostics and monitoring treatments11, as well as for patient stratification in clinical trials12 – but our 60

understanding of what contributes to the predictive value of the circulating proteome remains limited. A few 61

overlapping mechanisms could explain the widespread associations between plasma proteins and incident 62

disease outcomes: (1) plasma proteins have direct causal effects on disease onset; (2) plasma proteins are 63

impacted by disease processes that begin before disease diagnosis; and (3) plasma proteins are impacted by 64

external factors, like environmental exposures, that both contribute to disease onset and affect protein levels. 65

Gaining a deeper understanding of the specific roles of proteomic biomarkers in disease prediction has important 66

implications for the potential clinical utility of these biomarkers. 67

68

First, plasma proteins with causal effects on disease may be candidates for novel therapeutic targets. Several 69

disease-specific studies have investigated the potential causal roles of plasma proteins, including for type II 70

diabetes13, cardiometabolic diseases10,14,15, psychiatric disorders16,17, and gastrointestinal diseases18,19. 71

Phenome-wide studies across many diseases and phenotypes have also investigated the causal basis of 72

protein-disease associations20,21. These studies have identified putative drug targets such as SCARA5 for 73

cardioembolic stroke15 and IL1RL1 for inflammatory bowel diseases20. 74

75

On the other hand, non-causal plasma proteins may serve as biomarkers for monitoring disease onset and 76

progression. For example, a study on plasma proteomic biomarkers of dementia found that abundances of 77

certain predictive proteins began changing years before diagnosis22. Non-causal plasma proteins may also 78

work has speculated that the plasma proteome captures environmental effects7,23, and a handful of studies 80

investigating factors contributing to the variance of individual proteins have found that environmental exposures 81

can explain a substantial portion of variability in the levels of certain proteins24,25. However, major gaps remain 82

in understanding how modifiable factors contribute to the utility of the overall proteome as disease predictors. In 83

particular, few studies to date have simultaneously evaluated putatively causal proteins alongside other 84

mechanisms that may explain the predictive value of non-causal associations. In this study, we aimed to conduct 85

a comprehensive characterization of the relationships between plasma proteins and key disease outcomes in 86

order to delineate proteins as potential therapeutic targets or non-causal biomarkers of environmental risk 87

factors. 88

89

Utilizing blood proteomic data available from a subset of the UKB-PPP cohort (N = 45,438, see Methods), we 90

investigated an expanded set of associations between 2,923 unique proteins and 23 age-related incident disease 91

outcomes (see study design in Figure 1). We first applied Mendelian Randomization (MR) to partition the 92

disease-associated proteomic biomarkers into those with potential causal roles across diseases (i.e. drivers) vs. 93

non-causal roles (i.e. predictors). Next, we examined the impacts of smoking on the plasma proteome because 94

of its large environmental effect on disease risk. Integrating the MR and smoking analyses, we identified that a 95

large proportion of protein predictors are exposure-associated and likely play no causal role in disease 96

pathogenesis. To further evaluate the sensitivity of the plasma proteome to smoking, we developed a proteomic 97

score for smoking, and tested this score alongside smoking status and other clinical biomarkers in disease 98

prediction models. By replicating this proteomic score in an external dataset (FinnGen), we highlight the 99

objective, quantitative, and generalizable nature of environmental risk quantification enabled by proteomics. 100

Finally, we confirmed the generality of this paradigm by developing and testing an additional proteomic score for 101

alcohol intake, which is nearly entirely independent from the smoking protein score. 102

Results 118

Plasma proteins are widely associated with incident disease 119

Previously, we tested associations between levels of 1,468 plasma proteins, measured in UKB-PPP participants, 120

and 23 incident diseases over a 15-year follow-up period using Cox proportional hazards (PH) models. In this 121

study, we expanded these analyses to include associations with an additional 1,455 proteins (total proteins = 122

2,923), measured in the same individuals. Details on the plasma protein measurements, QC procedures, and 123

UKB-PPP sample have been described previously6 (see also Methods). We found 9,308 significant associations 124

between 2,122 proteins and 22 of the 23 incident disease outcomes, adjusting for age and sex variables 125

(Bonferroni-adjusted P-value < 0.05/(23*2923) = 7.44 x 10-7) (Supplementary Table 1). The number of 126

associations ranged from 1 association each for ALS, multiple sclerosis, colorectal cancer, and major depressive 127

disorder to 1,653 and 1,798 for liver disease and type 2 diabetes, respectively; brain/CNS cancer showed no 128

significant protein associations (Extended Data Fig. 1). 129

A small subset of proteins have causal effects on disease 141

To identify which subset of the thousands of protein-disease associations discovered represent potentially causal 142

relationships, we applied two-sample Mendelian Randomization (MR). 19 of the 23 disease outcomes that we 143

tested in the Cox PH models had suitable GWAS summary statistics for MR, as they did not include UKB data 144

which was used to identify genetic instruments (Supplementary Table 2). These diseases are the focal set for 145

subsequent analyses. We leveraged the catalog of protein quantitative trait loci (pQTLs) that were previously 146

mapped to these proteins6 to first subset to proteins with robust genetic instruments. To minimize potential 147

biases, we restricted genetic instruments to cis-pQTLs, and retained the proteins with F-statistics > 10 and that 148

passed Steiger filtering. Ultimately, 2,907 of the significant protein-disease pairs (involving 782 unique proteins) 149

had genetic instruments and were tested for causality via MR (Supplementary Table 3). 150

151

Only 225/2,907 protein-disease pairs (8%) showed suggestive evidence for causality (P-value < 0.05) (Figure 152

2a). In additional sensitivity tests for horizontal pleiotropy using MR-Egger26, we found that 9 of the 225 nominally 153

significant protein-disease pairs may have pleiotropic genetic instruments (Supplementary Table 4), and thus 154

further validation of these pairs may be needed. Overall, these cis-MR analyses did not reveal causal roles for 155

the majority of the proteins identified in observational associations, indicating that the vast majority of protein- 156

disease associations likely cannot be explained by causal effects of the protein on disease onset. 157

158

Among the 225 protein-disease pairs, we replicated known causal relationships such as proprotein convertase 159

subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9) and ischaemic heart disease27, and apolipoprotein E (APOE) and Alzheimer’s 160

disease28. Other protein-disease pairs with significant causal associations in this study and prior evidence for 161

causality included tumor necrosis factor receptor superfamily member 6B (TNFRSF6B) and inflammatory bowel 162

disease (IBD)29, peptidylglycine alpha-amidating monooxygenase (PAM) and type 2 diabetes30, and transforming 163

growth factor beta 1 (TGFB1) and ischaemic heart disease31. Sortilin1 (SORT1) had robust and significant 164

evidence for causal effects on type 2 diabetes in this study and its potential causal role has not been previously 165

identified. 166

167

We assessed the disease specificity of causal drivers identified in MR compared to the non-causal, disease- 168

associated predictors. We found that hundreds of non-causal predictor proteins were associated with multiple 169

diseases in the Cox PH models; several were associated with 9 or more diseases (e.g., amphiregulin (AREG), 170

ribonuclease A family member k6 (RNASE6), and CUB domain-containing protein 1 (CDCP1)). The diseases 171

associated with these highly non-specific proteins are involved in a broad range of mechanisms and pathways 172

(Figure 2b). In contrast, most of the causal driver proteins (172/198, 87%) were associated with 1 disease. On 173

Many protein-disease associations are driven by smoking 190

Given the widespread sharing of non-causal predictor proteins across diverse diseases, we next tested the 191

hypothesis that these proteins broadly associate with incident disease due to their associations with 192

environmental risk factors, and thus reflect environmental impacts without directly causing disease. Previously 193

developed proteomic scores for the incident disease outcomes showed better or similar prediction performance 194

compared to models comprised of age, sex, and other lifestyle factors, including BMI, alcohol intake, social 195

deprivation, educational attainment, physical activity, and smoking status7, pointing to a potential role of the 196

plasma proteome in partially capturing the effects of these risk factors. For lung cancer and COPD specifically, 197

we observed that incremental models with disease proteomic scores had minimal improvement beyond smoking 198

status (Extended Data Fig. 2). Previous literature, including studies using small, targeted microarrays, suggests 199

that smoking may alter plasma protein levels32,33. Thus, we further investigated the relationship between the 200

To first gauge the overall effects of smoking on the plasma proteome, we characterized the relationships between 204

self-reported smoking status and the 2,923 proteins measured in the UKB-PPP cohort, adjusting for age and sex 205

variables. 1,673 proteins (57%) were significantly associated with smoking status (Bonferroni-adjusted P-value 206

< 1.7 x 10-5) (Supplementary Table 5). 30 proteins measured in the Olink panel mapped to 21 plasma proteins 207

previously found to be associated with smoking32 (Supplementary Table 6), and all were significantly associated 208

with smoking in these analyses. 209

210

We then evaluated the effects of smoking on the disease-associated proteins specifically. All 178 proteins 211

associated with lung cancer in the Cox PH models were significantly associated with smoking, as were between 212

82-97% of proteins associated with all other diseases examined (Figure 3a), a notable enrichment beyond the 213

proportion of all measured plasma proteins associated with smoking. Additionally, we found that all proteins 214

associated with 8 or more diseases in the Cox PH models were smoking-associated, compared to smaller 215

proportions of the more disease-specific proteins (Figure 3b). 216

217

After adjusting for self-reported smoking status in the Cox PH models, 8,326 out of 9,308 (89%) protein-disease 218

pairs remained significant (Supplementary Table 7). Lung cancer showed the most substantial drop in the 219

number of associated proteins after adjustment (from 324 to 33 proteins, representing a 90% decrease); COPD 220

also showed a large decrease (from 1,501 to 1,250 proteins, representing a 17% decrease). Of note, most of 221

the remaining lung cancer-associated proteins (28/33, 85%) had significantly attenuated hazard ratios after 222

smoking adjustment (Wald test, p-value < 0.05), with a mean attenuation of 48.3% of the |𝑙𝑜𝑔(𝐻𝑅)|. Taken 223

together, these results indicate that although adjusting for smoking status yields large attenuations in the number 224

of associated proteins for some diseases, basic measures of smoking may fail to capture the full effects of 225

smoking in protein-disease associations. 226

227

Given the clear biological impacts of smoking, we then sought to systematically distinguish causal driver proteins 228

from exposure-associated predictor proteins, focusing on the 782 disease-associated proteins with valid genetic 229

instruments. We found that the vast majority of these proteins (N=640) were significantly associated with smoking 230

status. Moreover, most of these smoking-associated proteins (N=469) showed no evidence for causal effects on 231

disease from the cis-MR analyses (Figure 3c). Several proteins (N=171) were both associated with smoking 232

and nominated by MR, indicating that these proteins may represent (or be correlated with) causal mediators 233

between smoking and incident disease. 234

Another group of disease-associated proteins were neither associated with smoking nor showed evidence for 236

causality (Figure 3c). The majority of proteins in this group (86/115, 75%) were associated with 1 to 3 diseases 237

in the Cox PH models, potentially representing a group of proteins enriched for non-causal, disease-specific 238

predictors tagging incident disease processes. For example, 5 proteins in this group were associated with only 239

COPD, including a transmembrane activin inhibitor (BAMBI) that was previously found to be involved in 240

Based on these groupings, we characterized the proteins selected in our previously developed proteomic scores 243

Proteomic score quantifies smoking behavior and history 279

The widespread effects of smoking on the plasma proteome indicate that plasma proteins themselves may serve 280

as precise, quantitative measures of the cumulative biological effects of smoking and other exposures. To assess 281

the utility of the plasma proteome as a quantitative readout of smoking, we developed a smoking protein score 282

(SmokingPS). Since many of the measured proteins are likely correlated, we performed variable selection via 283

294

We compared the distributions of the SmokingPS across individuals in UKB-PPP who reported current, previous, 295

and never smoking status. As expected, the previous smokers had a SmokingPS distribution between the current 296

and never smokers (Figure 4a). We then stratified the previous smokers by years since smoking cessation and 297

pack years, which captures both quantity and frequency of smoking. As years since smoking cessation 298

increased, the distributions of the SmokingPS in previous smokers shifted towards the never smokers (Figure 299

4b). As illustrated by the SmokingPS distributions across individuals who stopped smoking recently, the 300

smoking-associated proteome starts to revert back to non-smoking levels within a couple years of smoking 301

cessation; this pattern is also observed from the levels of the top-weighted proteins in the SmokingPS, averaged 302

across bins of years since smoking cessation in former smokers (Extended Data Fig. 5). Similarly, those who 303

smoked fewer pack years had SmokingPS distributions closer to the never smokers (Extended Data Fig. 4b). 304

Stratifying current smokers by pack years reflected the same trend – individuals who reported fewer pack years 305

had SmokingPS distributions closer to, or overlapping, that of previous smokers (Figure 4c). The average 306

number of cigarettes smoked per day among current smokers ranged from 8.6 in the lowest quantile of 307

SmokingPS distribution to 20.1 in the highest quantile, underlining that the amount of smoking has a dose- 308

response impact on plasma protein levels (Extended Data Fig. 4c). 309

310

We further tested the value of this SmokingPS for disease prediction (Figure 4d, Extended Data Fig. 6). Among 311

the 19 incident disease outcomes, adding smoking status to baseline variables of age, sex, and genetic principal 312

components (PCs) resulted in the greatest improvement in performance for lung cancer, COPD, and liver 313

disease (delta C-index between baseline model vs. baseline with smoking status: 0.141, 0.083, and 0.024, 314

respectively). Adding the SmokingPS to the baseline model with smoking status further improved performance 315

Discussion 448

Our study shows that a substantial proportion of plasma protein-disease associations identified in observational 449

studies are the result of systemic effects of environmental risk factors on protein expression and do not reflect 450

causal relationships between those proteins and disease. Instead, our results suggest that much of the predictive 451

value of the disease-associated proteome stems from its association with environmental impacts, which have 452

been historically challenging to evaluate consistently across studies using objective and quantitative approaches. 453

This has significant implications for the clinical translation of disease risk estimates and biomarkers derived from 454

plasma proteomics, as it indicates that in many cases the proteins may be capturing the effects of an upstream 455

exposure driving changes in protein expression rather than directly contributing to disease onset. Our approach 456

can be applied to numerous diseases and exposure types, helping delineate how plasma proteomic information 457

can inform health interventions. 458

459

Associations between protein levels and disease incidence observed in epidemiological studies are susceptible 460

to confounding and other biases. We leveraged MR to determine which subset of protein-disease associations 461

may represent direct, causal effects of proteins on disease onset. Many prior studies have focused on identifying 462

causal proteins for specific diseases10,13,14, whereas our study investigated 19 different diseases that span 463

common metabolic diseases (e.g. type 2 diabetes), immune-mediated diseases (e.g. rheumatoid arthritis and 464

IBD), and cancers to discern potential patterns or differences in the proportions of causal proteins identified 465

their potential causal roles are critical to mechanistically characterize as they may constitute promising 474

therapeutic targets. 475

476

In the Cox PH models associating proteins with incident disease, we observed that many proteins were 477

associated with multiple, often unrelated, diseases. One explanation is that environmental factors that impact 478

shared pathways underlying many diseases also have widespread effects on the plasma proteome. In this study 479

we explored this scenario and focused on smoking as an example of a known environmental risk factor for many 480

diseases with persistent biological effects37. By integrating the MR and smoking analyses, we determined that 481

for many proteins tested for causal effects on disease, their associations with incident disease outcomes are 482

merely coincidental due to their independent associations with smoking. Our partitioning framework illustrates a 483

strategy for honing in on the proteins that may be most relevant to disease – whether as putative therapeutic 484

targets for pharmacological intervention (i.e. causal drivers), as quantitative sensors of environmental influences 485

on disease (i.e. exposure-associated predictors), or alternatively as biomarkers of disease-specific processes 486

beginning before diagnosis (i.e. non-causal predictors without smoking or other environmental exposure 487

association). We note that our study is not an exhaustive investigation of potential environmental perturbations, 488

and thus future work applying our approach to other environmental risk factors will enable further refinement of 489

these groups. Based on our finding that disease-based proteomic scores for lung cancer and COPD were largely 490

composed of smoking-associated predictors, other disease-based proteomic scores may similarly include non- 491

specific signals of other exposures that have extensive effects on the plasma proteome. 492

493

We developed a proteomic score for smoking that demonstrates the potential of the plasma proteome to provide 494

precise biomarkers of environmental risk factors. Distributions of the SmokingPS among previous and current 495

smokers demonstrated the dynamic nature of the plasma proteome, sensitive to not only smoking status but also 496

intensity and duration of smoking. This points to the ability of the plasma proteome to serve as an accurate and 497

detailed proxy for smoking behavior and history in addition to, or even instead of, questionnaire data. For 498

example, we identified a group of individuals in UKB who were labeled as current smokers but had a SmokingPS 499

discriminate between current and never smokers with an AUC of 0.9838. Studies have found that methylation 508

The SmokingPS was also associated with incidence of several diseases, particularly diseases for which smoking 519

is a known risk factor. The addition of the score to the smoking status variable offered modest improvements in 520

We note several limitations. First, although we obtained the largest GWAS publicly available without UKB data 539

for estimating the effects of genetic instruments on disease outcomes, limits in sample sizes may have limited 540

statistical power for estimating effects in MR. Second, we adopted several strategies to ensure the robustness 541

of the MR results, but violations of model assumptions are still possible; thus, potential causal drivers identified 542

in this study will require further validation. Third, we utilized data from only European ancestry populations for 543

the MR analyses, potentially limiting generalizability of the findings to other groups, although causal genetic 544

effects are largely shared across populations45,46. Fourth, the proteins captured by these proteomic assays are 545

not a completely random subset of the proteome; therefore, proteins involved in certain disease-specific 546

pathways may not be represented or below limits of detection, and proteins involved in general disease activity 547

may be disproportionately represented. Finally, we did not explore the possibility that some of the disease- 548

associated proteins may be biomarkers of early disease processes that begin prior to diagnosis due to limitations 549

in EHR data. A key challenge for deeply curated clinical cohorts will be distinguishing between effects from 550

unmeasured environmental factors and those arising from uncharacterized disease mechanisms. 551

552

In conclusion, we highlight the environment as a prominent component of the reported predictive power of the 553

disease-associated plasma proteome for patient outcomes. This underscores the challenge of interpreting 554

proteomic data, given that environmental exposures, alongside inherited genetic variation and ongoing disease 555

processes, have substantial impacts on plasma proteins. Drawing insights into disease-specific mechanisms 556

from this data will require systematic characterizations to separate true causal disease signals from more general 557

reflections of smoking or other factors. This is critical for not only understanding disease biology but also 558

improving disease prediction, since models with more disease-specific proteomic biomarkers may be more 559

portable across populations. Especially as the breadth of protein measurements are increasing at decreasing 560

cost, clarifying the roles of plasma proteomic measurements from these biobank datasets will be an important 561

step towards clinical translation. 562

563

Our work also suggests that proteomic assays may open up a path toward measuring the impacts of the 564

environment on human health and disease. Assessing genetic risk is now largely straightforward, thanks to 565

assays that enable consistent, reproducible measurements across studies. However, this has not been the case 566

for studies of environmental risk factors, where data tends to be collected using non-standardized questionnaires 567

Methods 579

Proteomic profiling in the UK Biobank 580

The UK Biobank Pharma Proteomics Project (UKB-PPP) is a precompetitive biopharmaceutical consortium 581

formed with the goal of collecting and characterizing the plasma proteomic profiles of participants from the UKB47, 582

a population-based cohort comprising approximately 500,000 individuals from the United Kingdom. The UKB 583

has been described in Bycroft et al.47 and details on the data available in the UKB can be found at 584

https://biobank.ndph.ox.ac.uk/showcase/. 54,219 participants were selected for the UKB-PPP cohort; we 585

restricted the sample used for these analyses to participants within the cohort who were randomly sampled from 586

the main UKB population. The Olink Explore 3072, an antibody-based proximity extension assay, was used to 587

measure the abundance of protein analytes in each plasma sample. Measurements were provided in the 588

Normalized Protein eXpression (NPX) values on a log2 scale. Full details on sample selection, the Olink assay, 589

and data processing and quality control are described in Sun et al.6. We excluded three proteins missing in >10% 590

of the sample (CTSS, NPM1, and PCOLCE), and imputed protein expression values of the remaining proteins 591

using the miceforest package in Python. All proteins except those missing in >30% of participants were used as 592

predictors for the imputation of each protein. We imputed a single dataset using a maximum of five iterations. All 593

other parameters were left at default values. After imputation, proteomic data were normalized separately within 594

each cohort by first rescaling values to be between 0 and 1 using MinMaxScaler() from scikit-learn and then 595

centering on the median. The final dataset consisted of 2,923 proteins measured in 45,438 individuals. 596

Mendelian Randomization 661

To determine the subset of protein-disease associations identified by the Cox PH models that also potentially 662

represent causal relationships, we performed two-sample Mendelian Randomization (MR). We used protein 663

quantitative trait loci (pQTLs) as genetic instruments, which had been previously identified from GWAS of the 664

2,941 protein analytes measured in 34,557 individuals of European ancestry in the UKB-PPP cohort6. We first 665

mapped pQTLs to the GRCh38/hg38 build and selected any genome-wide significant pQTL (P-value < 5x10-8). 666

We then excluded pQTLs located within the human major histocompatibility complex (MHC) region on 667

chromosome 6 (positions 28510120 to 33480577), due to the complex LD structure in this region, and on the 668

sex chromosomes. We additionally excluded pQTLs with MAF <= 0.005 and an INFO score <= 0.8. 669

670

We restricted our analyses to the cis-pQTLs, defined as those on the same chromosome and within 1Mb of the 671

transcriptional start site of the protein-coding gene. SNPs were allowed to be cis-pQTLs for one or more proteins. 672

To identify independent cis-pQTLs, we applied clumping in PLINK (v1.9b7-x86_64) for each protein, using an 673

LD threshold of r2 <= 0.001 and a reference panel including the 34,557 individuals of European ancestry from 674

the UKB-PPP GWAS of protein levels6. To prevent underflow, -log10(P-values) across proteins were scaled to 675

the [0,1] range before clumping. 676

677

Genetic association data for the outcomes were selected based on exclusion of UKB data, to avoid overlap with 678

the UKB-PPP cohort. 19 of the 23 disease outcomes had publicly-available GWAS that did not include UKB data 679

and included only individuals of European ancestry, or were available in the FinnGen study36 (freeze 10). To 680

boost power, we performed a meta-analysis of GWAS from FinnGen and Okada et al.52 for rheumatoid arthritis 681

(RA) using the METAL software53. For outcome GWAS without minor allele frequency (MAF) information, which 682

is required to perform Steiger filtering, we extracted MAF data from the non-Finnish European ancestry group 683

(NFE) in gnomAD v4.1.054. For the rheumatoid arthritis meta-analysis, the MAF used was computed as follows: 684

(MAFFinnGen*NFinnGen + MAFgnomAD_NFE*NOkada_2014)/(NFinnGen + NOkada_2014), where FinnGen refers to the FinnGen 685

GWAS for RA and Okada_2014 refers to Okada et al.52. The full list of outcome GWAS can be found in 686

Supplementary Table 2. 687

We additionally excluded cis-pQTLs with F-statistics <= 10, and performed Steiger filtering to exclude variants 691

with larger correlations with the outcome than the exposure.  Ultimately, we tested 2,373 protein-disease pairs 692
